title.en: Define flow of control and name its three kinds
Trace the output of simple decision programs

say.en: Every morning you decide: if it is raining, take an umbrella, else leave it at home. A program makes decisions in the same way, using the if statement. In this lesson: Define flow of control and name its three kinds.
Write if and if..else statements.
Trace the output of simple decision programs.

body.en: The order in which the statements of a program are executed is called the *flow of control*. Python supports three kinds: sequence (statements run one after another, top to bottom), selection (a condition decides which block runs) and repetition (a block runs again and again).

say.en: The order in which the statements of a program are executed is called the flow of control. Python supports three kinds: sequence (statements run one after another, top to bottom), selection (a condition decides which block runs) and repetition (a block runs again and again). Sequence: one statement after another.

say.en: Selection: if, if..else, if..elif..else.
Repetition: for and while loops.

title.en: On the board: if..else as a flowchart

say.en: A decision is drawn as a diamond. The condition inside it is either True or False.
If the condition is True, we follow the True arrow and print Even.
If it is False, we follow the other arrow and print Odd. Only one of the two blocks ever runs.
Both paths join again, and the program continues with the next statement in sequence.
In Python: the keyword if, a condition, a colon, and an indented block. The same for else.

body.en: The if statement runs a block only when its condition is True: if condition: followed by an indented block. The if..else statement chooses between two blocks: the if block runs when the condition is True, otherwise the else block runs. A condition is a Boolean expression built with relational operators such as >, <, ==, != and logical operators and, or, not.

else:  → block runs when the condition is False

tagline.en: Ask a yes-or-no question, then pick a path — just like Bolt at the fork.

myth.en: The computer runs both the if part and the else part.

truth.en: Exactly one branch runs: the first one whose question is answered yes (or else, if none are). The rest are skipped.

title.en: Bolt reaches a fork in the road

say.en: Bolt is going out. One road leads to an umbrella, the other to sunglasses. Which way should he go?
At the fork, Bolt asks one question: is it raining? The answer can only be yes or no.
It is raining, so the answer is yes. Bolt takes the left road and grabs the umbrella.
On a sunny day the answer is no. Else means: if the answer was no, do this instead. Bolt takes the right road.
In code we write if, the question, then what to do. Only one of the two paths ever runs. The other is skipped.
Need more than two choices? Elif means else if: ask another question. Bolt checks each question in order and stops at the first yes.

limits.en: A real driver also watches for people, other cars and sirens. A program only checks the exact condition you wrote, at the moment that line runs — if you forget a case, the computer won't think of it for you.

problem.en: Write a program that prints the positive difference of two numbers num1 = 5 and num2 = 12 (the larger minus the smaller).

narration.en: The condition num1 greater than num2 is False, so the else block subtracts num1 from num2.

say.en: The condition num1 greater than num2 is False, so the else block subtracts num1 from num2. Write a program that prints the positive difference of two numbers num1 equals 5 and num2 equals 12 (the larger minus the smaller).
num1 equals 5.
num2 equals 12.
if num1 is greater than num2.
diff equals num1 - num2.
else.
diff equals num2 - num1.
print("Difference =", diff).
So the answer is Difference equals 7.
